lines.text: $\hl{1}{15^2} = \hl{2}{9^2 + 12^2}$, so by the converse of Theorem 14 the angle opposite the side of length $15$ is a right angle.

problems.note: Changed from the last problem: the converse now says two equal angles give equal sides (not squares), and the answer is a perimeter. The method is the same: state the converse, use it to match sides, then use the result.

steps.ask: The theorem goes from equal sides to equal angles. What does the converse go from and to?
steps.title: State the converse

lines.text: The converse is: if two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal.

steps.ask: Which side is opposite ∠P, and which side is opposite ∠Q?
steps.title: Apply it

lines.text: $\hl{1}{\angle P}$ is opposite $[QR]$ and $\hl{2}{\angle Q}$ is opposite $[PR]$. These angles are equal, so the sides are equal.

steps.ask: Which three side lengths do you now know, and what do they add up to?
steps.title: Add the three sides

problems.note: Changed from the last problem: this uses a corollary of the angle sum theorem rather than a converse, so the answer comes from adding two angles rather than matching sides. The steps are: name the two interior opposite angles, add them, then check with the straight-line angle.

steps.ask: Which two interior angles are opposite the exterior angle at the third vertex?
steps.title: Use the corollary

lines.text: The exterior angle at the third vertex equals the sum of the other two interior angles (the interior opposite angles).

steps.ask: The third interior angle and the exterior angle lie on a straight line. What do they add up to, and what is the third interior angle?
steps.title: Check with the theorem

lines.text: The third angle is $180 - 47 - 58 = 75^\circ$. It lies on a straight line with the exterior angle.
